title: Why a phone gets warm even when it is not plugged in
text: A phone does not need a charger to get hot. Almost all of the electrical energy a phone draws from its battery ends up as heat, because the chip, the screen, the radios and the battery itself are all imperfect converters of energy into useful work. When the phone is unplugged, that energy comes out of the battery instead of out of the wall, but the heat it produces is the same heat. Charging is simply one more source of warmth on top of the others, and a phone that is busy while unplugged can easily run hotter than a phone that is idle while charging. The practical consequence is that the question to ask about a warm phone is not whether it is plugged in, but what it is doing. Heavy processing, a bright screen, a struggling radio and a hot room all add heat independently, and they add up. A phone is a sealed device with no fan, so the only way that heat leaves is by spreading through the frame and the back cover and then into the air or your hand. If heat arrives faster than it can escape, the temperature rises until something gives.

title: Games and graphics work are the largest single source of heat
text: Three dimensional games are the most demanding thing most people ask a phone to do. They keep the graphics processor busy drawing a new frame many times a second, they keep several processor cores busy running game logic and physics, and they usually keep the screen at high brightness and a high refresh rate at the same time. All three draw power continuously, and a game can hold that load for as long as you keep playing, which is quite unlike the short bursts of work involved in reading a message or loading a web page. Sustained load matters more than peak load. A phone can run its processor flat out for a few seconds without warming noticeably, because the metal in the frame absorbs the heat. Over several minutes that reserve is used up and the surface temperature climbs. This is why a phone often feels fine for the first few minutes of a game and uncomfortably warm after twenty. Higher frame rate settings, higher resolution settings and demanding graphics options all increase the amount of work per second, so lowering them is one of the most effective ways to reduce heat without stopping play.

title: Recording video heats a phone quickly
text: Recording video is one of the hardest sustained jobs a phone does. The camera sensor runs continuously, the image processor corrects and stabilises every frame, the video encoder compresses the result in real time, and the storage system writes a steady stream of data to flash memory. All of these run at once, for as long as you keep recording. Higher resolutions and higher frame rates increase the work sharply: recording at 4K and 60 frames per second moves several times as much data per second as recording at 1080p and 30 frames per second, and the encoder and the storage have to keep up with all of it. Many phones will warn you during long recordings at the highest settings, and some will stop recording to protect themselves. Recording outdoors in sunlight is the worst case, because the screen is also at maximum brightness so that you can see the viewfinder, and the sun is warming the body of the phone directly. If a phone becomes hot while filming, lowering the resolution or frame rate, moving into shade, and letting it rest between clips all help.

title: Watching video: streaming warms a phone more than local playback
text: Watching video warms a phone, though usually less than recording it. Three things draw power: the screen, which is on continuously and often bright; the video decoder, which turns compressed data back into pictures; and the network radio, if the video is being streamed rather than played from storage. Modern phones have dedicated decoding hardware that handles common video formats very efficiently, so decoding itself is rarely the main problem. Streaming adds the radio to the picture, and the radio is often the larger cost of the two, especially on a weak mobile connection where the phone must transmit at higher power to stay connected. This is why the same film can warm a phone noticeably more when streamed over patchy mobile data than when downloaded first and played back offline. If a phone becomes uncomfortably warm during long viewing, downloading episodes in advance over home wifi, lowering the streaming quality, and reducing screen brightness all reduce the heat produced. Holding the phone in a stand rather than in your hand also helps, because your hand is both insulating the back of the phone and noticing the warmth.

title: The camera app heats a phone even when you are not taking photos
text: An open camera app is doing continuous work whether or not you press the shutter. The sensor is capturing frames, the phone is running autofocus and exposure adjustments, and the live preview is being processed and drawn on the screen many times a second. Leaving the camera open while deciding on a shot therefore costs almost as much as recording. Taking a photo adds a short, intense burst of processing on top. Modern phone photography is computational: a single press may capture several frames at different exposures and combine them, remove noise, sharpen detail and apply portrait or night mode effects. Night mode is particularly demanding because it captures and aligns many frames over several seconds. Taking a long series of photos in quick succession gives the phone no time to cool between bursts, and the processor and image signal processor stay busy continuously. If a phone gets hot during a long photo session, closing the camera app between shots rather than leaving it open makes a measurable difference, and so does turning off the most demanding modes when conditions do not require them.

title: On-device artificial intelligence features generate heat
text: Phones increasingly run machine learning models locally rather than sending data to a server. Speech recognition, live translation, photo subject recognition, text summarisation, background blur in video calls and generative image editing can all run on the handset. Running them locally is good for privacy and works without a network connection, but the computation has to happen somewhere, and that somewhere is the phone. These models involve large numbers of arithmetic operations, and while phones now include dedicated neural processing hardware that is far more efficient than a general purpose processor for this work, efficient is not the same as free. A large model producing a long answer can keep that hardware busy for several seconds continuously, and repeated requests keep it busy indefinitely. The heat produced is real and is one of the genuine costs of moving computation onto the device. It is also why on-device systems benefit from deciding how much work to do based on the state of the phone: doing less work when the device is already hot trades a little quality for a temperature the phone can sustain.

title: Background apps and synchronisation keep a phone working while idle
text: A phone that is sitting on a table with a dark screen is not necessarily idle. Email, messaging, social media, cloud photo backup, fitness tracking and file synchronisation applications all wake up periodically to check for new data, upload what has changed, and refresh their content. Each wake-up is short, but there may be many applications doing it, and each one involves waking the processor from its low power state and usually switching on a radio. A phone that never gets to stay asleep for long will be warmer and will lose charge faster than one that does. Photo and video backup deserves particular mention, because uploading a large batch of recordings combines sustained processor work, sustained radio transmission and sustained storage reads for as long as the upload takes. If a phone is warm with the screen off, the battery usage screen in settings will usually name the applications responsible. Restricting background activity for applications that do not need it, and allowing large backups to run only on wifi and overnight, both reduce the heat produced during the day.

title: Downloads, app updates and system updates produce bursts of heat
text: Installing applications and system updates is short term but intense work. The phone downloads a large amount of data over the network, writes it to storage, verifies it, decompresses it and then often optimises the installed code for the specific device. The last step can keep several processor cores busy for some minutes, which is why a phone may be warm for a while after an update has finished downloading, when it looks from the outside as though nothing is happening. This also explains a common pattern: a phone that suddenly runs hot and loses charge quickly for a day or two after a major system update, then settles down. After an update the system often rebuilds search indexes, re-optimises installed applications and reprocesses the photo library. That work is finite. If the warmth persists for more than a few days of normal use, it is worth investigating further rather than waiting, because at that point it is more likely to be a misbehaving application than the normal post-update housekeeping.

title: A weak mobile signal makes the radio work much harder
text: The mobile radio in a phone adjusts its transmission power according to how well it can reach the nearest cell tower. With a strong signal it can transmit quietly and still be heard. With a weak signal it must transmit at much higher power, and it may also retry transmissions that fail, which multiplies the cost. This is why a phone can become noticeably warm in a basement, a lift, a thick walled building, a train travelling through countryside, or anywhere at the edge of coverage, even when you are not actively using it. The phone is working hard simply to stay registered on the network. Constantly moving between coverage areas has a similar effect, because the phone repeatedly searches for and connects to new towers. If a phone is warm and the signal indicator shows one or two bars, the radio is a likely explanation. Switching to wifi where it is available, or enabling flight mode in a place with no usable coverage, stops the radio from repeatedly trying and allows the phone to cool.

title: 5G, mobile data and why the network choice matters for temperature
text: Newer mobile network generations move data faster, but speed and efficiency are not the same thing. 5G in particular can use higher frequency bands that do not travel as far or penetrate buildings as well, so a phone may be at the edge of coverage more often and transmit at higher power when it is. Some phones also maintain connections to more than one network generation at once, which means more radio hardware is active. The result is that 5G can run warmer than 4G in areas where 5G coverage is patchy, while being comparable or better where coverage is strong. Heavy data use compounds this, because the radio is active continuously rather than in brief bursts. If a phone becomes warm while using mobile data, and especially if the coverage is poor, setting the preferred network type to 4G can reduce the heat produced without any noticeable loss for ordinary use. Using wifi instead of mobile data where it is available is usually better still, because wifi transmits over much shorter distances at much lower power.

title: Navigation combines several heat sources at once
text: Turn by turn navigation is demanding because it runs several expensive things simultaneously and continuously. The satellite positioning receiver is active throughout, the mobile radio downloads map tiles and traffic information, the screen is on at high brightness so that it can be read in daylight, and the processor continuously redraws the moving map. A navigation session therefore warms a phone much more than its individual parts would suggest. The environment usually makes this worse rather than better. A phone mounted on a windscreen or dashboard sits in direct sunlight behind glass, which is one of the hottest places in a car, and the airflow around a mounted phone is poor. Many people also find their phone is warm after navigating even on a short journey for this reason. Mounting the phone away from direct sun, aiming an air vent at it, downloading maps for offline use in advance, and lowering the screen brightness all reduce the heat. If the phone is charging from the car at the same time, that is an additional source of warmth on top of all of these.

title: The screen is one of the biggest consumers of power in a phone
text: The display is often the single largest consumer of battery power in ordinary use, and the energy it uses becomes heat. Brightness is the main factor: running a screen at full brightness can consume several times as much power as running it at a comfortable indoor level. Outdoors in sunlight a phone will raise brightness automatically to remain readable, which is exactly when the sun is also warming the phone directly, so the two effects arrive together. Screen size and refresh rate also matter. A high refresh rate display redraws the image more often, which costs power both in the display itself and in the graphics hardware that has to produce the extra frames. On phones with OLED screens the content matters too, because these displays illuminate each pixel individually and dark images use less power than bright ones. Reducing brightness, letting automatic brightness do its job rather than fixing it at maximum, shortening the screen timeout, using a dark theme on an OLED phone, and lowering the refresh rate where the option exists all reduce both heat and battery drain.

title: A hot environment reduces the phone's ability to shed heat
text: A phone cools itself by passing heat from its frame and back cover into the surrounding air. How quickly that happens depends on the difference between the phone's temperature and the air's temperature. On a warm day that difference is smaller, so the same workload leaves the phone hotter. In a hot car or a room without ventilation, the surrounding air may already be warmer than the phone can comfortably tolerate, and the phone may heat up while doing almost nothing. Direct sunlight is a separate and stronger effect, because the phone is absorbing energy from the sun rather than merely failing to shed its own. A dark phone left face up on a table in the sun can reach a surface temperature far above the air temperature around it. The combination of a hot environment and direct sun is the most common cause of a phone overheating while apparently idle. Moving the phone into shade, keeping it out of a closed car, and not leaving it on a windowsill or a car dashboard all address this directly and quickly.

title: Cars are a difficult environment for phones
text: The inside of a parked car in sunlight can become far hotter than the air outside, because sunlight passes through the glass and the heat it produces cannot escape. A phone left in such a car, particularly on a dashboard or a seat in direct sun, can reach temperatures well beyond anything it would encounter in normal use. Phones protect themselves in this situation by displaying a temperature warning and shutting down most functions until they cool, and repeated exposure of this kind shortens battery life permanently even when no immediate damage is visible. Using a phone while driving adds further heat on top of a hot starting point, because navigation, music streaming and charging usually all run at once. The practical advice is simple: do not leave a phone in a parked car in hot weather, mount it away from direct sunlight when using it for navigation, point an air vent at it if the car is hot, and if it displays a temperature warning, stop using it and let it cool rather than trying to continue.

title: Cases and covers slow down cooling
text: A phone sheds heat through its outer surfaces, so anything covering those surfaces slows that process down. A thick protective case, especially a rugged one with foam or rubber layers, acts as insulation. The phone still produces the same amount of heat, but it escapes more slowly, so the internal temperature climbs higher before it reaches balance. The phone may then reduce its own performance to compensate, which is why the same game can run noticeably less smoothly in a heavy case. Thin cases made of harder materials interfere much less. The effect is most noticeable during long demanding sessions rather than ordinary use: for checking messages the difference is negligible, while for a long game, a long video recording or a long navigation session it can be the difference between comfortable and uncomfortably hot. If a phone becomes hot during demanding use, taking the case off for the duration is one of the simplest things that helps, and it works immediately. Resting the phone on a hard surface rather than on a bed, a sofa or a cushion helps for the same reason.

title: An aging battery produces more heat for the same work
text: Lithium ion batteries change as they age. Their capacity falls, so they store less energy, and their internal resistance rises. Internal resistance is the part that matters for heat: every time current flows out of the battery, some energy is lost inside the battery itself and turns into heat there. As resistance rises with age, the same current produces more of this internal heating than it did when the battery was new. The result is a phone that feels warmer than it used to during the same activities, loses charge faster, and may shut down unexpectedly when the voltage drops under load even though the indicator shows charge remaining. Most phones report battery health in settings, usually as a percentage of the original capacity. A figure that has fallen substantially, combined with unexpected warmth and sudden shutdowns, points to the battery rather than to software. Battery ageing is accelerated by heat, which creates a feedback loop: a hot phone ages its battery faster, and an aged battery runs hotter. Replacing a worn battery often restores both the running temperature and the battery life.

title: A single misbehaving application can keep a phone busy indefinitely
text: Most unexplained heat in an otherwise idle phone comes from one application that is not behaving as it should. An application with a programming fault may enter a loop that keeps a processor core busy continuously, may repeatedly retry a network request that keeps failing, or may hold a wake lock that prevents the phone from entering its low power state at all. From the outside this looks like a phone that is warm and losing charge with the screen off and nothing obviously running. The battery usage screen in settings is the place to look. It lists applications by the power they have consumed over a period and usually distinguishes foreground from background use. An application near the top of that list that you have barely opened is the likely culprit. Force stopping it will confirm the diagnosis: if the phone cools and the drain stops, the application was responsible. The durable fix is to update it, restrict its background activity, or uninstall it. Restarting the phone often clears the symptom temporarily, which is useful for confirming a diagnosis but is not a solution if it returns.

title: Malicious software and hidden mining
text: Some unwanted software deliberately uses a phone's processor for its own purposes. Cryptocurrency mining code attempts to run calculations continuously for as long as it can, which means a phone that is hot and losing charge rapidly while apparently doing nothing. Advertising fraud software loads advertisements invisibly in the background, which combines processor use with constant network activity. Neither announces itself, and both are designed to be hard to notice. The warning signs are a phone that is persistently hot with the screen off, battery life that has fallen sharply without any change in how the phone is used, high data use that does not match your activity, and in some cases applications you do not remember installing. This is more likely on phones where applications have been installed from outside the official store, and more likely on phones that are no longer receiving security updates. The response is to check the battery and data usage screens for unfamiliar names, uninstall anything unrecognised, run a scan with a reputable security application, install any pending system updates, and in a serious case back up personal data and reset the phone.

title: Heat that starts right after a software update
text: It is common for a phone to run hotter than usual for a short period after a major system update, and this is usually normal. After the update the system rebuilds search indexes, re-optimises installed applications for the new version, and often reprocesses the photo library for features such as face and object recognition. This is a large amount of work, it runs in the background, and it typically finishes within a few days of ordinary use. Leaving the phone on wifi and connected to power overnight lets much of it complete while the phone is not needed. Heat that persists beyond that is a different matter. An update can also introduce a fault, or leave an application incompatible with the new system version, and either can produce a process that never settles. If a phone is still unusually hot a week after an update, the battery usage screen will usually identify the component or application responsible. Updating all applications, clearing the cache of the application named, or as a last resort backing up and resetting the phone are the usual remedies.

title: What thermal throttling is and why a hot phone feels slow
text: Phones monitor their own temperature with sensors placed near the processor, the battery and the outer casing. When those sensors report temperatures approaching the safe limits, the system reduces the speed of the processor and graphics hardware so that less heat is produced. This is called thermal throttling, and it is a protective measure working correctly rather than a fault. The visible effects are a phone that becomes slower the longer it is used for something demanding: a game that ran smoothly for ten minutes begins to stutter, video recording stops at the highest quality settings, the camera refuses to use the most demanding modes, and charging slows or pauses. Some phones also dim the screen. The phone is choosing reduced performance over rising temperature, which is the correct trade. Throttling is a signal worth paying attention to. If a phone throttles during ordinary tasks that it used to handle without difficulty, that suggests the cooling path is compromised, the battery has aged, or something is running in the background that should not be.

title: Warm, hot and too hot: judging whether a temperature is normal
text: Warmth is not by itself a fault. A phone that is noticeably warm during a game, a long video call, navigation or a large download is behaving normally, and the warmth should fade within minutes once the activity stops. A useful test is whether the temperature matches the work. Warm while doing something demanding is expected; warm while sitting untouched on a table with the screen off is not. The second test is comfort. A phone that is warm to the touch is fine. A phone that is uncomfortable to hold against your skin, or too hot to keep in a trouser pocket, has gone beyond normal operating temperature and the activity causing it should be stopped. The third test is behaviour. Temperature warnings on screen, the camera refusing to open, charging pausing, the screen dimming on its own, sudden shutdowns or rapid unexplained battery drain all indicate the phone is at or beyond its limits. Any of these together with heat deserves attention rather than being waited out, and the signs described in the guidance on dangerous symptoms should be checked.

title: What to do when a phone is too hot right now
text: The first step is to stop the work that is producing the heat. Close games, camera, navigation and video applications rather than leaving them in the background. Move the phone out of direct sunlight and out of a hot car. Take it out of its case, which allows heat to escape much faster, and rest it on a hard surface rather than on a bed, a sofa or a cushion, both of which insulate it. Lower the screen brightness or turn the screen off. If the phone is charging, unplug it. If the signal is poor and the phone is struggling to connect, turn on flight mode for a few minutes, which stops the radio from transmitting at high power. Do not try to cool a phone quickly. Putting it in a refrigerator or freezer, running it under cold water or applying ice risks condensation forming inside the device and causing damage that is worse than the heat. A phone left alone in a cool room will return to normal temperature in a matter of minutes, and that is the right approach.

title: Settings and habits that keep a phone cooler over time
text: Several ordinary settings reduce the heat a phone produces during a normal day. Use automatic screen brightness rather than fixing it at maximum, and shorten the screen timeout. If the phone offers a high refresh rate display, consider setting it to adapt or to a lower rate. Restrict background activity for applications that do not need to run constantly, and schedule photo and video backup for wifi and for overnight. Keep applications and the system updated, because many heat problems are fixed in updates. Remove applications you no longer use, which removes their background activity along with them. Prefer wifi over mobile data where it is available, and consider setting the preferred network to 4G if 5G coverage is patchy where you spend most of your time. Use a thinner case, or take the case off for long demanding sessions. For navigation, download offline maps and mount the phone away from direct sunlight. None of these changes is dramatic on its own, and the phone will still get warm when asked to do demanding work, which is normal. Together they reduce the amount of time it spends unnecessarily warm.

title: A swollen battery is a serious warning sign
text: A battery that has begun to swell is a genuine hazard and should never be ignored. The signs are visible: the back cover or the screen starts to lift away from the frame, the phone no longer sits flat on a table and rocks when pressed at a corner, gaps appear around the edges of the case, or the screen bulges. Swelling happens when a damaged or worn lithium ion cell produces gas inside its sealed pouch, and it is often preceded by a period of running unusually hot. A swollen battery can rupture, and a ruptured lithium cell can catch fire. If a phone shows any of these signs, stop using it and stop charging it immediately. Do not press on the bulge, do not try to prise the phone open, and do not puncture the battery under any circumstances. Keep the phone away from anything flammable, and take it to a repair centre or a proper battery disposal point. Do not put a swollen battery in ordinary household waste. A swollen battery is not something that improves on its own and the phone should not be used until it is replaced.

title: When heat means stop using the phone
text: Most warmth in a phone is harmless, but a few symptoms mean the phone should be stopped and examined rather than used. Stop immediately if the phone is too hot to hold comfortably and does not cool within a few minutes of being left alone, if it shuts down on its own because of temperature and does so more than once, if the back cover or the screen is lifting or bulging, if the phone smells of burning or of a sharp chemical odour, if the screen is discoloured or distorted in a way that was not there before, or if the phone becomes hot while doing nothing at all and a check of the battery usage screen shows nothing responsible. Prolonged contact with a hot phone can cause skin burns, particularly while asleep, so a phone should not be left in a bed or under a pillow. In any of these cases, stop using the phone, unplug it, keep it away from flammable materials, and have it inspected. Sudden shutdowns at moderate charge levels together with unusual heat usually point to a battery that has reached the end of its life.

title: Heat usually has more than one cause at once
text: In practice a phone that is uncomfortably hot is rarely suffering from a single problem. The common situations combine several sources. Navigating in a car on a sunny day runs the satellite receiver, the mobile radio, the screen at full brightness and the processor, in an environment that is already hot and where airflow is poor. Filming an outdoor event runs the camera, the encoder and the storage, with the screen bright and the sun on the phone. Playing a game on a train combines sustained graphics work with a mobile radio that is repeatedly switching between towers at the edge of coverage. This is why the fix is usually a combination too, and why removing just one of the causes often produces a surprisingly large improvement: the phone only needs to shed heat slightly faster than it produces it to settle at a lower temperature. It is also why diagnosing an unexplained hot phone is best done by elimination. Note what is running, what the environment is, how strong the signal is and how old the battery is, then remove the easiest factor first and see whether the phone settles.

title: Which parts of a phone actually produce the heat
text: Heat in a phone does not come from one place. Four parts produce most of it. The main chip, which contains the processor cores, the graphics hardware and the neural accelerator, is the largest source under load and is also the smallest in area, so it reaches the highest temperatures. The display is the largest consumer in ordinary use, and because it covers the whole front of the phone its heat is spread out rather than concentrated. The mobile radio produces heat in proportion to how hard it has to transmit, which depends on signal strength rather than on anything the user chose. The battery produces heat internally whenever current flows in or out of it, and more so as it ages. The power management circuits add a smaller amount of their own, because converting one voltage to another is never completely efficient. Knowing which part is working explains why two phones that feel equally hot can behave very differently: a phone hot from its chip will slow down, while a phone hot from its radio will not, because the radio's heat does not trigger the same protective response.

title: How a phone gets rid of heat without a fan
text: A phone has no fan and no vents, so every bit of heat it produces has to travel outwards through solid material and then into the air or into whatever is touching it. Manufacturers spread that heat deliberately. Sheets of graphite, copper foil and in some phones a sealed vapour chamber move heat sideways away from the chip, so that no one point on the case becomes painfully hot and so that a larger area is available to release it. The metal frame of the phone acts as both a spreader and a radiator. This design has an important consequence: a phone can absorb a burst of heat without feeling warm, because the metal soaks it up, but it cannot do that indefinitely. Once the spreading material is at the same temperature as the chip, the only thing left is how fast heat crosses into the surrounding air, and that is slow. This is why demanding work feels fine for a few minutes and uncomfortable after twenty, and why anything that covers the case makes a long session noticeably worse.

title: The case can feel mild while the inside is very hot
text: A phone reports more than one temperature, and they can differ by a great deal. The skin or case sensor measures the outer surface, which is what a hand feels and what the phone uses to decide whether it is uncomfortable to hold. Separate sensors sit next to the main chip, the battery and the charging circuit, and these read the inside. Under heavy load the gap between them can be large, because the chip is small and hot while the case is wide and only warm. A phone whose case reads a mild temperature may have an internal zone far above it. This matters for anyone judging a phone by touch. A case that feels merely warm is not proof that nothing is near a limit, which is why a phone can begin slowing down or refusing to record video while still feeling comfortable in the hand. It also matters for anyone measuring a phone: a reading means little without knowing which sensor produced it, and the surface and the interior are not interchangeable numbers.

title: How to find out how hot your own phone is
text: Most phones do not show a temperature to the user, but the information is usually reachable. The battery section of the settings app sometimes reports battery temperature, and the phone's own diagnostics menu may show more. Some manufacturers include a device care or hardware test screen that lists sensor readings. Third-party monitoring applications read the same sensors the system does and present them continuously, which is useful for watching a trend rather than a single value. On a phone connected to a computer, the developer tools can print every thermal zone the hardware exposes, which is the most complete view available and the one that shows how far apart the surface and the interior can be. Two cautions are worth keeping in mind. First, a single number means nothing without knowing which sensor it came from. Second, monitoring applications themselves consume power and keep the screen on, so watching the temperature continuously will raise it slightly. For diagnosing a persistent problem, the battery usage screen, which names the applications responsible, is more useful than any temperature reading.

title: Sharing your connection makes a phone work unusually hard
text: Using a phone as a mobile hotspot is one of the most demanding things it can do, and it is easy to underestimate because the screen is usually off. The phone runs two radios at once: the mobile radio receiving data from the network, and the wifi radio transmitting it to the connected devices while also acting as an access point. Both run continuously for as long as the hotspot is on, and the processor handles the routing between them. Unlike a game, there is no natural stopping point, so the load persists for hours. The result is a phone that becomes hot, loses charge very quickly, and may reduce its own performance or shut the hotspot down to protect itself. Tethering over a cable instead of wifi removes one of the two radios and helps considerably. Placing the phone somewhere with air around it, rather than in a bag or under a laptop, helps too, as does keeping the screen off and the phone out of direct sun, since a hotspot session often happens in a car or outdoors.

title: Video calls run almost everything at once
text: A video call is unusual in combining nearly every expensive subsystem a phone has. The camera captures continuously, the encoder compresses the outgoing video, the decoder expands the incoming video, the screen stays on to display it, the radio transmits and receives throughout, and the processor handles echo cancellation, noise suppression and increasingly background blur or replacement. Each of these on its own is a moderate load. Together, and sustained for the length of the call, they produce more heat than most games. Long calls therefore warm a phone considerably, and a phone held in the hand during the call feels it more because the hand both insulates the back and senses the warmth directly. Several things reduce it. Turning the camera off converts the call into an audio call and removes the two most expensive parts. Turning off background blur removes a continuous processing task. Using wifi rather than mobile data lowers the radio cost. Propping the phone in a stand rather than holding it lets the case shed heat into the air instead of into a hand.

title: Why wifi usually runs cooler than mobile data
text: For the same amount of data, a wifi connection usually costs a phone less power than a mobile connection, and the reason is distance. A home or office access point is a few metres away, so the phone can transmit very quietly and still be heard. A cell tower may be hundreds of metres or several kilometres away and behind walls, so the phone must transmit far harder to reach it. Transmission power is the dominant cost in both cases, so the shorter link wins. There are exceptions worth knowing. A wifi network at the far edge of its range is no better than a weak mobile signal, and a phone struggling to hold a distant access point will be warm for exactly the same reason. A phone that can see a saved network but cannot quite connect may also retry repeatedly, which is worse than either. In general, though, preferring wifi where it is strong, and downloading large files over wifi rather than mobile data, both reduce the heat a phone produces and extend how long its battery lasts.

title: Bluetooth is rarely the reason a phone is hot
text: It is worth knowing which things are not significant causes of heat, because chasing the wrong one wastes effort. Bluetooth is one of them. The low-energy variant used by headphones, watches, fitness bands and trackers was designed for devices that run for days or months on tiny batteries, and it transmits at a small fraction of the power a mobile radio uses over a range of a few metres. A phone paired with a watch and a pair of earbuds all day is not meaningfully warmer for it. Audio streaming to headphones costs slightly more than a watch connection, because data flows continuously, but it remains small next to the screen or the mobile radio. There are two caveats. Transferring a large file over Bluetooth is slow and keeps the radio active for a long time, which does add up. And a companion application for a watch or a tracker may itself misbehave and keep the processor busy, in which case the application rather than the Bluetooth connection is the cause. The battery usage screen distinguishes the two.

title: What flight mode actually turns off, and when it helps
text: Flight mode switches off every radio in the phone at once: the mobile modem, wifi and Bluetooth, and on most phones satellite positioning as well. Because the mobile radio is often the largest consumer in a phone that is otherwise idle, this can make a substantial difference, but only in specific circumstances. It helps most where there is little or no usable coverage. In a basement, a lift, a remote area or a building with thick walls, the phone repeatedly searches for a network and transmits at maximum power when it finds a weak one, and all of that effort achieves nothing. Switching the radios off stops it and lets the phone cool. It helps least where coverage is strong, because a phone with a good signal transmits quietly and the radio is not the problem. Flight mode will not help at all with heat from a game, a video recording or a bright screen, since none of those involve a radio. If a phone is hot while idle and the signal indicator shows one bar, flight mode is worth trying first.

title: Why lithium-ion batteries dislike heat
text: The lithium-ion cell in a phone works best at roughly the temperatures people find comfortable, and both extremes are bad for it. Cold temporarily reduces the power it can deliver, which is why a phone in winter may shut down suddenly and then recover indoors. Heat does something worse: it permanently accelerates the chemical reactions that degrade the cell. Those reactions consume the materials that store charge and thicken the layers that carry it, so a battery kept hot loses capacity faster and never gets it back. This is why temperature matters more for long-term battery life than the number of times a phone has been charged. A phone used hard and kept hot for a year can lose noticeably more capacity than one used gently. It also explains why phones refuse to charge when they are very hot or very cold, and why they slow charging as they warm: the protection is worth more than the few minutes saved. Keeping a phone out of hot cars and direct sun, and not using it for demanding work while it is already hot, are the practical ways to protect it.

title: Heat and battery wear make each other worse
text: There is a loop between temperature and battery condition that explains why heat problems tend to get worse rather than stay the same. Heat ages a battery: it accelerates the reactions that reduce capacity and raise internal resistance. A battery with higher internal resistance produces more heat for the same current, because more energy is lost inside the cell itself. That extra heat ages it further. The loop is slow, taking months or years rather than days, but it is the reason a phone that ran warm when new often runs hot after two summers of heavy use, with battery life falling at the same time. Two practical conclusions follow. First, managing temperature early is worth more than it appears, because the benefit compounds over the life of the phone. Second, when a phone has clearly entered this state, with poor battery life, unusual warmth during ordinary tasks and occasional unexpected shutdowns, replacing the battery addresses the cause rather than the symptom, and usually restores the running temperature as well as the battery life.

title: What charging adds, and why a phone can be hot without it
text: Charging is a real source of heat, and separating it from the others is what makes the unplugged case clear. When a phone charges, energy moves from the charger into the battery and some of it is lost along the way: in the charging circuit that converts the incoming voltage, and inside the cell itself as current flows in. Fast charging pushes more current and therefore loses more, which is why phones are warmest during the first part of a fast charge and why charging deliberately slows as the battery fills or warms. Wireless charging is less efficient again, because energy crosses an air gap between two coils and what does not make it across becomes heat in both devices. None of this is required for a phone to get hot. Everything else a phone does, from running a game to holding a weak mobile signal, produces heat on its own, and while unplugged that energy comes out of the battery instead. A phone can easily be hotter while busy and unplugged than while idle and charging, and the activity rather than the charger is what decides.

title: Not all processor work costs the same
text: A phone processor is not one processor. It contains several kinds of core: a small number of large, fast ones, and a larger number of small, efficient ones, sometimes with a middle tier as well. The system decides which work goes where. Scrolling a list or checking for new mail runs on the efficient cores and costs very little. A game, a video export or a large application update runs on the fast cores, which do far more work per second and consume far more power to do it. This is why two tasks that both show the processor as busy can produce completely different amounts of heat, and why a percentage figure alone is a poor guide. It also explains a common surprise: a phone can feel cool while apparently busy, because the work is being handled entirely by efficient cores. The practical consequence is that reducing a demanding task matters much more than reducing a trivial one. Closing a handful of idle background applications saves very little, while lowering a game's graphics settings or shortening a long export saves a great deal.

title: Large file operations and encryption produce heat
text: Writing and reading large amounts of data warms a phone in two ways: the flash storage itself consumes power, and the processor does work on every byte that passes through. Modern phones encrypt their storage, so all of that data is encrypted on the way in and decrypted on the way out. Dedicated hardware makes this efficient, but it is not free when the volume is large. Noticeable cases include copying a large collection of photos or videos to or from a computer, restoring a backup onto a new phone, installing a large game, and the first indexing pass after a system update when the phone reprocesses its whole photo library. Each of these moves gigabytes rather than megabytes and runs for minutes rather than seconds. A phone restoring a backup will be hot and will lose charge quickly, and that is expected rather than a fault. The sensible approach is to let large transfers run when the phone is not needed, out of its case and not in direct sun, rather than while carrying it in a pocket.

title: Always-listening features and what they cost
text: A phone that responds to a spoken wake phrase is listening continuously, which sounds expensive and usually is not. The listening is handled by a very small, dedicated low-power processor that does nothing but compare incoming sound against one or two patterns. It consumes a tiny amount of power and does not wake the main processor until it thinks it has heard the phrase. The cost arrives after that. Once triggered, the phone wakes fully, turns on the screen, may run speech recognition on the device, and usually contacts a server, which involves the radio. A phone that is triggered repeatedly by background conversation or television will therefore be warmer and lose charge faster, not because it is listening but because it keeps waking up. Dictation is a different matter: continuous speech recognition for minutes at a time is real sustained work. If a phone is unexpectedly warm and the assistant's activity log shows many triggers that were not intended, turning the wake phrase off removes both the false wakes and the privacy question that comes with them.

title: Scrolling a feed is more demanding than it looks
text: Scrolling a social media feed does not feel like demanding work, but it combines several costs continuously. The screen is on and usually bright. Videos autoplay as they come into view, so the video decoder runs almost constantly and the radio downloads the next ones before they are reached. High refresh rate displays redraw the moving content more often. Some applications also pre-load far ahead, which means downloading content that is never seen. Because feeds have no end, this continues for as long as the session lasts, and half an hour of scrolling can warm a phone as much as a shorter period of gaming. Three settings help. Turning off video autoplay, or restricting it to wifi, removes both the decoding and much of the downloading. Lowering the screen brightness reduces the largest single consumer. Using the application's data-saver option, where it exists, reduces how much is fetched ahead. None of these changes what the application is for, and together they make a long session noticeably cooler and longer on a charge.

title: Augmented reality and camera effects are among the heaviest tasks
text: Augmented reality applications and live camera effects are close to the most demanding things a phone can run. The camera captures continuously, the phone tracks either the surrounding space or a face in three dimensions, the graphics hardware renders objects aligned to what the camera sees, and the screen displays the result at a high frame rate. Depth sensors and multiple cameras may run at the same time. Every one of these is active simultaneously and continuously, which is why measuring a room with an AR tool, playing an AR game or using live face effects in a video call warms a phone quickly. Phones usually protect themselves during these sessions by lowering the frame rate, reducing tracking quality or dimming the screen, and the effects often become visibly less smooth after a few minutes. That is the protection working rather than the application failing. Short sessions with gaps between them, a phone out of its case and out of direct sunlight, and lower quality settings where the application offers them all make the experience more consistent.

title: Older phones running newer software
text: A phone several years old often runs warmer than it did when new, even with the same applications, and there are two separate reasons that are easy to confuse. The first is the battery, which has lost capacity and gained internal resistance, so it produces more heat for the same current and lasts less time between charges. The second is software. Applications and system versions grow more demanding over time, adding features and effects designed for newer hardware, so an older chip has to work proportionally harder to do what looks like the same job. The two causes need different responses, which is why distinguishing them is worth the effort. A battery health figure that has fallen substantially, together with unexpected shutdowns, points to the battery, and replacing it is usually both cheaper and more effective than replacing the phone. Warmth that tracks specific heavy applications, with battery health still reasonable, points to software, and the remedies are the ordinary ones: lower graphics settings, lighter alternatives to the heaviest applications, and removing what is no longer used.

title: Where a phone sits changes how hot it gets
text: A phone sheds heat into whatever surrounds it, so its position matters as much as its workload. Air carries heat away slowly but steadily. Fabric does not: a phone in a trouser pocket, a closed bag, under a pillow or on a duvet is wrapped in an insulator, and the same work leaves it considerably hotter than it would on a table. Body heat adds to this, since a pocket against the leg starts from skin temperature rather than room temperature. The worst combinations are the common ones. A phone navigating or streaming while in a pocket or a bag is doing sustained work with no way to release the heat. A phone left charging on a bed overnight is both producing heat and insulated on every side, and this is the situation in which phones have caused burns and scorching. The remedies are simple and immediate: put the phone on a hard surface while it is working hard, take it out of a bag during a long navigation session, and never leave it under bedding or a pillow.

title: Common beliefs about phone heat that are not true
text: Several widely repeated remedies do not work, and two of them cause damage. Cooling a hot phone quickly in a refrigerator or freezer, under cold water or against ice is actively harmful: the rapid change causes moisture to condense inside the device, and liquid damage is worse than the heat it was meant to cure. A phone left alone in a cool room recovers in minutes, which is all that is needed. Closing every application in the recent-applications list does not help either. Applications in that list are mostly suspended and consuming nothing, and on some systems closing them makes things worse, because each one has to be fully restarted the next time it is opened. Applications advertised as cooling or memory-boosting tools cannot lower a temperature; they consume power themselves to display a reading, and many exist to show advertisements. Finally, warmth during demanding work is not itself a defect to be fixed. The things that genuinely help are reducing the work, improving the airflow, and dealing with a specific misbehaving application or a worn battery.

title: Humid and still air make cooling harder
text: Air temperature is not the only property of the surroundings that affects how a phone cools. Moving air carries heat away far faster than still air, which is why a phone in a closed room feels hotter during a long session than the same phone near an open window or a fan, even at the same air temperature. Humidity matters for the person more than for the phone: damp air makes a warm surface feel hotter against the skin and slows the body's own cooling, so a phone that is objectively no warmer than usual can feel worse in humid weather. Very humid conditions bring a separate risk, which is condensation when a cool phone is brought into warm damp air, and most phones will refuse to charge until the port is dry. The practical points are modest but real. A phone doing sustained work benefits from being somewhere with air movement, out of a bag and off soft furnishings, and a phone that has been somewhere cold should be allowed to reach room temperature before it is charged.

title: Freeing up storage space on a phone
text: When a phone reports that storage is full, there are several places to look before deleting anything you might want later. Photos and videos are almost always the largest category, and moving them to a computer or a cloud service and then removing the local copies frees the most space for the least effort. Downloaded video and music for offline viewing is the next largest, and is easy to re-download later. Application caches can grow large over time, particularly for social media and messaging applications, and most phones offer a storage screen that lists applications by size and allows caches to be cleared. Messaging applications also store every image and video ever received in a conversation, which accumulates quietly over years. Many phones include a storage assistant that suggests files to remove and can delete backed-up photos automatically. It is worth leaving some free space rather than filling the storage completely, because the system uses spare space for updates and for its own temporary files, and a phone with almost no free storage can behave unpredictably and refuse to install updates.

title: Composing a better photograph with a phone camera
text: Most of what makes a phone photograph good is decided before the shutter is pressed. Light is the most important factor: photographs taken with light falling on the subject are generally better than photographs taken with a bright window behind the subject, which leaves the subject in shadow. Soft light early or late in the day is more flattering for portraits than harsh light at midday. Composition comes next. Enabling the grid overlay in the camera settings helps with placing the horizon straight and with placing a subject off centre, which is usually more interesting than placing it in the middle. Getting closer to the subject is almost always better than using digital zoom, which simply crops the image and loses detail. Keeping the lens clean makes a surprising difference, because fingerprints produce a hazy image and visible flare around bright lights. Steadiness matters in low light, so bracing your elbows against your body or resting the phone on a solid surface will produce a sharper image than holding it at arm's length.

title: Pairing a Bluetooth device with a phone
text: Pairing is the process of introducing two Bluetooth devices to each other so that they will connect automatically afterwards. The accessory must first be put into pairing mode, which usually means holding a button until an indicator light flashes in a particular pattern. On the phone, open the Bluetooth settings screen, which will list nearby devices that are currently discoverable, and select the accessory by name. Some devices ask for a confirmation code to be matched on both sides. When pairing fails, the usual reasons are that the accessory was not in pairing mode, that it is already connected to another device nearby, that it is out of charge, or that it is still remembered by the phone from a previous pairing that has gone stale. Removing or forgetting the device on the phone and pairing it again from the beginning resolves most of these. Turning Bluetooth off and on, or restarting the phone, clears others. Accessories generally have a limit on how many devices they can remember, and pairing a new one may push an older one out of that list.

title: Choosing and fitting a screen protector
text: Screen protectors come in two main types. Tempered glass protectors are rigid, feel much like the original screen, and resist scratches well, but they can crack on impact and are thicker. Plastic film protectors are thinner and cheaper and will not shatter, but they scratch more easily and can feel less smooth. For a phone with a curved screen edge, a protector designed specifically for that model is important, because a flat protector will not adhere at the edges and will lift. Fitting one well is mostly about dust. Clean the screen thoroughly with the supplied wipe, then remove any remaining specks with a piece of sticky tape immediately before applying the protector, and work in a room where dust is not being disturbed. Align the protector carefully before letting it touch the screen, because repositioning it afterwards usually traps dust. Small bubbles at the edges often disappear over a day or two, while a bubble with a speck at its centre will not and means the protector should be lifted and the speck removed. Protectors that interfere with an under-display fingerprint reader should be registered again after fitting.

title: Transferring photographs from a phone to a computer
text: There are several ways to move photographs from a phone to a computer, and the right one depends on how many there are. For a small number, sharing them directly to a messaging application or an email to yourself is quickest. For a whole library, connecting the phone to the computer with a cable is the most reliable method: the phone will ask whether to allow the connection and what mode to use, and file transfer mode must be selected before the computer will show the phone's storage. The photographs are usually in a folder named for the camera. For regular ongoing transfers, a cloud photo service that synchronises automatically is more convenient, since new photographs appear on the computer without any action. Whichever method is used, it is worth verifying that the copy on the computer is complete and opens correctly before deleting anything from the phone. Keeping a second copy on an external drive protects against losing both at once, since a cloud service that synchronises deletions will remove a photograph everywhere if it is deleted in one place.

title: Setting up an email account on a phone
text: Most email providers are recognised automatically. Open the mail application, choose to add an account, enter the address and password, and the application will look up the correct server settings. Accounts protected by two factor authentication will ask for a code from an authentication application or a text message, and some providers require an application specific password to be generated instead of using the main account password. Manual setup is occasionally necessary for an employer or a smaller provider, and requires the incoming and outgoing server names, the port numbers and the security type, all of which the provider publishes. IMAP is the usual choice for incoming mail because it keeps the phone and other devices in step with each other; POP downloads messages to one device and is rarely the right option now. Once the account is working, the synchronisation frequency can be adjusted, and choosing a less frequent check or manual refresh for a rarely used account reduces background activity. Notification settings are usually separate per account, so an account can be synchronised without alerting you to every message.

title: Changing ringtones and notification sounds
text: Ringtones and notification sounds are set in different places, which is a common source of confusion. The ringtone is the sound for incoming calls and is set in the sound settings. Notification sounds are usually set per application, through the notification settings for that application, so changing the general notification sound will not alter the sound a particular messaging application makes. Many applications also have their own in-application sound setting that takes precedence over the system one. To use a custom audio file as a ringtone, the file generally needs to be placed in the ringtones folder on the phone's storage, after which it will appear in the list of available tones. A specific ringtone can also be assigned to an individual contact by editing that contact, which is useful for recognising important callers without looking at the phone. If a phone makes no sound at all, check whether it is in silent or vibrate mode, whether do not disturb is active and whether a schedule has switched it on automatically, and whether the volume for ringing is set separately from the volume for media.

title: Backing up contacts
text: Contacts are among the most difficult things to recreate if a phone is lost, so they are worth backing up deliberately. The simplest method is to store them in an account that synchronises automatically, so that they exist on a server as well as on the phone and appear on a replacement device as soon as the account is added. It is worth checking which account new contacts are being saved to, because a contact saved only to the phone or only to the SIM card is not included in that synchronisation and will be lost with the phone. The contacts application usually offers an export function that writes all contacts to a single file in the vCard format, which can be stored on a computer or an external drive and imported into almost any phone or mail program later. Doing this occasionally provides a copy that does not depend on any one service remaining available. Before relying on any backup, it is worth confirming that the exported file actually contains the expected number of entries and opens correctly, rather than assuming it worked.

title: Choosing a memory card for a phone
text: Phones that accept a memory card take the microSD format, and not every card is suitable for every phone. Capacity is the first consideration, and the phone's specifications state the largest size it supports. Speed is the second and is more often misunderstood. The large number printed on a card describes the fastest reading speed under ideal conditions, which is rarely the limiting factor in a phone. The more useful markings are the speed class symbols, which state a guaranteed minimum sustained writing speed, and a card used for recording high resolution video needs a class that guarantees enough sustained write speed for that format or recordings will stop unexpectedly. Buy from a reputable seller, because counterfeit cards that report a much larger capacity than they actually have are common and will appear to work until the real capacity is exceeded, at which point data is silently lost. Once fitted, a card can usually be used either as removable storage or formatted as internal storage, and the second option ties the card to that phone so that it cannot be read elsewhere.

title: What megapixels do and do not tell you about a camera
text: A megapixel is one million picture elements, and the megapixel count describes how many of them a camera sensor records. It therefore describes the size of the image, not its quality. A larger image can be cropped further or printed larger before detail runs out, which is a real benefit, but beyond a certain point the extra resolution exceeds what a small lens can usefully resolve and what most people will ever view. Several other factors influence how good a photograph looks. The physical size of the sensor matters, because a larger sensor collects more light and produces less noise in dim conditions. The lens aperture matters for the same reason. Optical image stabilisation allows longer exposures without blur. The processing applied afterwards has become at least as important as the hardware, since phones now combine several frames to reduce noise and extend the range between highlights and shadows. Many phones with very high megapixel counts combine groups of neighbouring pixels into one by default, producing a smaller image with better low light performance, which is a reasonable indication that more pixels is not simply better.

title: Choosing a lock screen method
text: Every phone offers several ways to unlock it, and they are not equally strong. A long passcode is the most secure and the least convenient. A pattern is quicker but can often be guessed from smudges on the screen or from someone watching once. A four-digit PIN is weak on its own, and a six-digit one is considerably better. Fingerprint and face recognition are convenient rather than independently secure: they unlock the phone using a code that is still stored underneath, which is why the phone asks for the passcode after a restart or after several failed attempts. Biometric methods also behave differently in practice. A fingerprint reader struggles with wet or very dry fingers, and face recognition may fail in darkness or with a mask. The sensible arrangement for most people is a six-digit PIN or a passphrase as the underlying secret, with a biometric method for everyday convenience. It is also worth checking which notifications appear on the locked screen, since message previews can reveal verification codes to anyone who picks the phone up.

title: Using do not disturb and notification schedules
text: Do not disturb silences notifications without turning the phone off, and most phones allow a great deal of control over the exceptions. A schedule can switch it on automatically at night and off in the morning. Specific contacts can be allowed through, which is the usual arrangement for family, and most phones have an option to let a second call from the same number within a few minutes ring, so that someone with a genuine emergency can reach you. Alarms almost always still sound, which is worth verifying rather than assuming. Separate profiles for sleeping, working and driving can each have their own list of exceptions, and the driving profile can switch on automatically when the phone connects to a car. If notifications are arriving when they should not, the usual causes are an exception that is broader than intended, an application marked as urgent, or a second schedule overlapping the first. If nothing is arriving when it should, the usual cause is a schedule that switched on and was never noticed, which is visible in the quick settings panel.

title: Sharing a wifi network with someone else
text: Most phones can pass a wifi password to another device without anyone reading it out. On a phone already connected, opening the network's details usually offers a share option that displays a QR code; the other person points their camera at it and joins. Between two phones of the same brand, or two phones signed in to accounts that know each other, the offer to share may appear automatically when the second phone comes near the network. For a visitor who needs access for longer, many home routers support a separate guest network with its own password, which keeps other devices on the home network out of reach. Where sharing fails, the usual reasons are that the two phones use different systems and need the QR code rather than the automatic offer, that the network is hidden and must be typed in by name, or that the router limits how many devices may connect at once. Printing the guest network's QR code and leaving it somewhere visible saves repeating the whole exercise for every visitor.

title: Physical SIM cards and eSIMs
text: A SIM identifies a subscriber to a mobile network. The traditional form is a small removable card, now usually the smallest nano size, fitted in a tray that opens with a pin. An eSIM does the same job without a card: the identity is written into a chip inside the phone, and a new one is added by scanning a code from the operator or through their application. Many recent phones support both, which allows two numbers at once, and some support only eSIM. Each form has practical consequences. A physical card moves between phones in seconds, which is convenient when replacing a handset or travelling with a borrowed device. An eSIM cannot be moved by hand and must be transferred through the operator, which takes longer, but it cannot be lost or damaged and can be bought and activated from abroad without visiting a shop. Travellers often use a local eSIM for data while keeping their usual number on the physical card. Before switching a phone, it is worth confirming that the operator supports the transfer method the new phone requires.

title: Reviewing which applications can use what
text: Applications must ask before using the camera, the microphone, location, contacts, photos and several other things, and those decisions can all be revisited later. The privacy section of settings lists permissions both ways: every permission with the applications that hold it, and every application with the permissions it has. Reading it the first way is more revealing, because seeing the full list of applications that may use the microphone usually turns up one or two that have no need for it. Several choices are available beyond yes and no. Location can be granted approximately rather than precisely, which is enough for weather and news. Access can be granted only while the application is in use, or once, so that a permission needed for a single task does not persist. Photo access can often be limited to selected images rather than the whole library. Most phones will also revoke permissions automatically from applications that have not been opened for some months, and will show an indicator when the camera or microphone becomes active.

title: Arranging the home screen and widgets
text: A widget shows information from an application directly on the home screen without opening it, such as the weather, a calendar for the day, a note or the controls for whatever is playing. Widgets are added by holding an empty area of the home screen and choosing from the list, and most can be resized afterwards by dragging a handle, which often changes how much detail they show rather than simply scaling them. Applications can be grouped into folders by dragging one onto another, and folders can be renamed. Several phones allow stacking widgets in one position so that they can be swiped through, or rotated automatically through the day. The number of rows and columns in the grid can usually be changed in the home screen settings, which is the quickest way to fit more on a screen or to make the icons larger. A useful habit is to keep the bottom row for the few applications used many times a day, since that row is the easiest to reach with one hand, and to leave the upper area for widgets.

title: Making text and interface elements easier to read
text: Phones offer more control over legibility than most people use. Font size is adjusted with a slider in the display settings and applies to most applications. A separate display size or zoom setting scales the whole interface, including buttons and icons, which is often more effective than enlarging the text alone because it keeps proportions sensible. A bold text option thickens every character, which can help more than making it larger. Beyond these, the accessibility section usually offers high contrast text, the removal of transparency effects, and an option to underline or outline links and buttons that are otherwise distinguished only by colour. Magnification gestures allow part of the screen to be enlarged temporarily by a triple tap, which is useful for small images or fine print inside an application that does not scale. A screen reader is available for those who need it, and a colour filter can be applied for colour vision deficiency. Changing the display size can make some application layouts shift unexpectedly, so it is worth checking the applications used most after adjusting it.

title: Setting up and using voicemail
text: Voicemail is provided by the mobile operator rather than by the phone, so the arrangements differ between networks. In most cases it is enabled by default and reached by holding the number one on the keypad or by dialling a short access number. A first use normally requires setting a passcode and recording a greeting, and the system prompts through both. Many operators and phones also offer visual voicemail, which lists messages like a mailbox so that any message can be played directly instead of listening through them in order, and sometimes provides a written transcript. Common problems have common causes. Messages that never arrive usually mean call forwarding to the voicemail number has been lost, often after moving the SIM to a new phone, and the operator can reinstate it. A forgotten passcode has to be reset by the operator, not on the phone. If a transcript is wrong, that is the transcription service rather than the recording, and the original audio can still be played in full.

title: Cleaning up duplicate contacts
text: Duplicate contacts appear when the same person is stored in more than one account, most often after adding a second email account or restoring a backup alongside contacts that were already synchronised. The contacts application usually offers to find and merge them: it groups entries it believes are the same person and asks for confirmation, after which the merged entry keeps every number and address from both. Reviewing the suggestions rather than accepting them all is worthwhile, because two family members who share a surname and a landline are sometimes grouped together, and separating them afterwards is more work than declining once. Choosing a single account to hold contacts prevents the problem recurring, and the setting for which account new contacts are saved to is usually in the contacts application's own preferences rather than in system settings. Contacts stored on the SIM card deserve a separate look: they are limited in what they can hold, are not included in account synchronisation, and are frequently the source of a stale duplicate that keeps returning after every cleanup.

title: Keyboard settings, autocorrect and text shortcuts
text: The on-screen keyboard has more settings than most people adjust. Autocorrect can be turned off entirely, or left on while its suggestions are rejected by tapping the original word in the suggestion strip, which also teaches it not to make that change again. Words it keeps getting wrong, such as names and places, can be added to a personal dictionary so that they are never corrected. A text replacement or shortcut list expands a few characters into a longer phrase, which is useful for an email address or a postal address typed often. Other options include swipe typing, where a word is drawn in one continuous motion, a number row shown permanently, and one-handed mode, which shifts the keyboard to one side. Several keyboards can be installed and switched between with the globe or keyboard key, which is how additional languages are added; autocorrect then works in whichever language is active. If predictions start suggesting embarrassing or irrelevant words, clearing the learned word history resets what the keyboard has picked up without changing any other setting.

title: Finding a lost phone
text: Both major phone systems include a service that locates a lost handset from any browser or from another device signed in to the same account. It shows the phone's last known position on a map, and offers three actions: make it ring, even if it is silenced, which finds it down the side of a sofa; lock it and display a message with a contact number on the screen; and erase it entirely, which should be the last resort because it usually ends any further tracking. The service only works if it was switched on beforehand, which it normally is by default, and it needs the phone to have power and some form of connection. Some systems can report a last position just before the battery dies, and some can locate a phone that is switched off through nearby devices. Two things are worth doing before anything is lost: confirm that the feature is enabled and that the account password is known, and make sure a trusted contact or a recovery method exists, since being locked out of the account prevents using the service at all.

title: Two-factor authentication on a phone
text: Two-factor authentication asks for something beyond a password when signing in, so that a stolen password alone is not enough. The common forms differ in strength. A code sent by text message is better than nothing but is the weakest, because a number can be moved to another SIM by someone impersonating the owner. A code generated by an authenticator application is stronger, since it is produced on the device itself and never travels. A passkey or a hardware security key is stronger still and also resists fake sign-in pages, because the credential is tied to the real site. Setting up an authenticator application takes a minute per account: the site shows a QR code, the application scans it, and a six-digit code then rotates every thirty seconds. The step people skip is saving the recovery codes offered during setup, which are the only way back in if the phone is lost, and they belong somewhere other than on that phone. Moving to a new handset is far easier with an authenticator that synchronises, or by re-enrolling each account before the old phone is wiped.

title: Basic photo editing on a phone
text: The editor built into most photo applications handles the adjustments that improve ordinary pictures. Cropping and straightening come first, because composition matters more than any adjustment of tone, and a horizon that is slightly tilted is the most common fixable flaw. Exposure or brightness corrects a picture that is too dark or too light overall, while separate highlight and shadow controls recover detail at one end without affecting the other, which is more useful than brightness for a picture taken against a bright window. Contrast and saturation are easy to overuse; small movements usually look better than large ones. A warmth or white balance control corrects the orange cast of indoor lighting. Automatic enhancement is a reasonable starting point and can be adjusted afterwards. Edits are almost always non-destructive, meaning the original is kept and the changes can be reverted at any time, which makes experimenting safe. A copy can be saved instead if a separate edited version is wanted, and this is worth doing before sharing, since some applications apply their own compression on upload.

title: Cables, connectors and data transfer speeds
text: Two cables with identical connectors can behave very differently, because the connector describes only the shape. A USB-C cable may support anything from slow data transfer to very fast transfer and video output, and nothing on the outside usually says which. Many cables supplied with phones carry power well but transfer data at the slowest rate, which is why copying a large video library can take far longer than expected with the cable that came in the box. If a phone is being connected to a monitor or a dock, the cable must support video, and many do not. Cable length matters as well, since the fastest rates are only guaranteed over short cables. For charging, the relevant property is how much power the cable and charger will negotiate, and a cable rated for a lower current will simply charge more slowly rather than fail. The practical approach is to keep one known good high-speed cable for data and for displays, label it, and use the rest for charging where the difference does not matter.
